items.statement:
Assume AC, $r\ge1$, and $\hbar>0$. Let $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$,
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$,
and let $W(z)$ be the regular irreducible Weyl system of
[[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. For every real
$S\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$, there is a unitary $M_S$ on
$L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ such that
$$M_S^*W(z)M_S=W(S^Tz)\qquad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r});$$
equivalently, $M_S^*RM_S=SR$ on the common transported Schwartz core.
Any two such implementers differ by a scalar of modulus one. The same
construction applies in every nonzero irreducible regular representation
with this finite phase space and fixed central parameter $\hbar$, after the
unitary equivalence of
[[thm-nrqmx-finite-weyl-uniqueness-interface]].

There is also a connected topological group
$\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ of normalized propagators of real
homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonians on this finite-mode Schrödinger space.
Here a unitary Schwartz automorphism means a unitary on $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$
whose restriction is a continuous linear bijection of the Schwartz space
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ with continuous inverse. A normalized propagator is defined on a compact interval $[0,T]$ with $0<T<\infty$. Its coefficient path $K:[0,T]\to M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ has Lebesgue-integrable entries and is symmetric, $K(t)=K(t)^T$ for every $t$; an almost-everywhere symmetric integrable path is understood through a symmetric representative. In the displayed interleaved quadrature order put
$$H_t=\frac14\sum_{a,b=1}^{2r}K_{ab}(t)(R_aR_b+R_bR_a)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r),$$
with no linear or scalar term. The path $U:[0,T]\to\mathcal U(L^2(\mathbb R^r))$ consists of unitary Schwartz automorphisms, has $U(0)=I$, and for every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ its trajectory $U(t)f$ is absolutely continuous in each Schwartz seminorm $p_{\alpha,\beta}(g)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta g(x)|$ and satisfies $i\hbar\,\partial_tU(t)f=H_tU(t)f$ almost everywhere. Absolute continuity in a seminorm means the finite disjoint-interval condition for the seminorms of the increments. The construction below proves existence, uniqueness and continuity of the inverse path in the same pointwise Schwartz topology. Precisely, $\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ is the set of all endpoint operators $U(T)$ for this integrable-coefficient class, over all such $T$ and $K$. Piecewise-smooth coefficient paths are included and yield the same endpoint set, as proved below; the definition does not restrict the admissible propagators to that subclass.
Give $\operatorname{Mp}$ the topology of pointwise convergence of $U$ and
$U^{-1}$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ in its Schwartz topology; give
$\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ its usual matrix topology.
The map
$$\pi:\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R),\qquad M\longmapsto S \quad\text{when }M^*W(z)M=W(S^Tz),$$
is a two-fold covering homomorphism. Its two points over $S$ act by $M_S$
and $-M_S$ when $M_S$ denotes either normalized lift; an arbitrary Weyl
implementer may differ from them by any scalar phase. This connected double
cover and its unitary action are the metaplectic group and metaplectic
representation. All mode counts here are finite; no infinite-mode
implementation claim is part of the statement.
items.proof:
1.1 Reorder interleaved coordinates by the fixed permutation $P(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)$, and write $R_g:=PR$ and $W_g(w)=W(P^Tw)$ for grouped labels. Then $J_0=PJP^T$ and $S_g=PSP^T$ obeys $S_g^TJ_0S_g=J_0$. Apply [F3] directly to the grouped Weyl system on $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ with label matrix $S_g^T$; this matrix is symplectic because $S_g^TJ_0S_g=J_0$ also implies $S_gJ_0S_g^T=J_0$. Since $S_g^TP=PS^T$, converting labels back gives $$M_S^*W(z)M_S=M_S^*W_g(Pz)M_S=W_g(S_g^TPz)=W(S^Tz).$$ Differentiating the bounded one-parameter Weyl identity on the common Schwartz core gives $M_S^*RM_S=SR$. For the rest of the proof abbreviate $R_g$ to $R$ and $S_g$ to $S$, so $R$, $K$, and $J_0$ all use grouped order. [A1, A2, F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 Use exactly the endpoint definition and trajectory class in the Statement, on arbitrary compact intervals $[0,T]$ with $T>0$. Reordering by the fixed permutation of step 1.1 sends $K$ to $PKP^T$ and preserves entrywise integrability, reality and symmetry, so [F4] constructs and uniquely determines these evolutions in grouped order with $H_t=\tfrac14\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}(t)(R_jR_k+R_kR_j)$ and no linear or scalar term. The operator acts on the common Schwartz space, and each trajectory is absolutely continuous in every seminorm and solves the equation almost everywhere. Concatenation gives products: first evolve by $U_2$ on $[0,T_2]$, then evolve by $U_1$ on $[0,T_1]$ with initial vector $U_2(T_2)f$, obtaining endpoint $U_1(T_1)U_2(T_2)$. The concatenated coefficient is integrable and symmetric on $[0,T_2+T_1]$, and the two absolutely continuous trajectories match at the join. The reversed evolution $U(T-t)U(T)^{-1}$ starts at $I$, ends at $U(T)^{-1}$, and is generated almost everywhere by $-H_{T-t}$, whose symmetric coefficient is again integrable. Thus inverses also belong to the set. By [F4], each endpoint implements the symplectic solution $\dot S=J_0K(t)S$. If two matrices had the same implementing unitary, differentiating their Weyl covariances on Schwartz space would give $(S-S')R=0$. Applied to the vacuum, $Q_kg_0=\sqrt{\hbar/2}g_{e_k}$ and $P_kg_0=i\sqrt{\hbar/2}g_{e_k}$ by [F6]; the reality of the rows forces both their position and momentum coefficients to vanish. Thus the endpoint is unique. For two lifts, $\pi(M_1M_2)=\pi(M_1)\pi(M_2)$ by conjugating the quadratures, so $\pi$ is a homomorphism. [F1, F4, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 Every generator from [F2] is a path endpoint of a homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonian. A symmetric shear is joined to the identity by scaling its symmetric block, and a partial Fourier rotation is joined by varying the oscillator angle. If $\det A>0$, polar decomposition writes $A=OP$ with $O\in SO(r)$ and $P$ positive definite. The path $P_t=(1-t)I+tP$ stays positive definite, and an orthogonal matrix in $SO(r)$ is a product of plane rotations, each joined to the identity by varying its angle. These paths connect the coordinate change to the identity. If $\det A<0$, factor one coordinate reflection from a positive-determinant change; that reflection is a $\pi$ oscillator rotation on that mode. This gives a piecewise-smooth symplectic path for each generator. Along any such path $S_t$, the matrix $X_t=\dot S_tS_t^{-1}$ satisfies $X_t^TJ_0+J_0X_t=0$; hence $K_t=-J_0X_t$ is symmetric and $\dot S_t=J_0K_tS_t$. The symmetrically ordered quadratic with matrix $K_t$ therefore has this classical endpoint. Thus [F2] supplies, for every $S$, a product of normalized quadratic propagators whose endpoint is $S$, proving $\pi$ is onto. The one-parameter paths also show that each such product belongs to the identity component of $\operatorname{Mp}$. [F2, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 If $M_1,M_2$ implement the same $S$, then [F3] makes $M_2M_1^*=\lambda I$ for some $|\lambda|=1$. For any other representation $W'$ in [F1], choose a unitary $V$ with $VW'(z)V^*=W(z)$ by the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem. Then $M'_S=V^*M_SV$ is unitary and $$M_S'^*W'(z)M'_S=V^*M_S^*W(z)M_SV=W'(S^Tz).$$ Conjugating the phase-uniqueness statement by $V$ proves the same result in that representation. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 If two normalized lifts lie over the same grouped matrix $S$, the Gaussian determinant calculation in [F5] makes them differ by sign. This already holds for every $S$: the matrix $A+iB$ used there is invertible by symplecticity, including when either real block is singular. In particular it supplies the required invertible-$B$ chart argument without an imported Maslov-index parity formula. Thus every fiber has at most two elements. [F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The identity has two distinct lifts. The constant zero Hamiltonian gives $I$. On the first mode (and as the identity on the other modes if $r>1$), take the canonical Schwartz evolution of $H=\hbar(N+1/2)$ constructed in [F4]. For each Hermite vector, $e^{-it(n+1/2)}|n\rangle$ solves the same Schrödinger equation with that initial vector, so uniqueness in [F4] identifies $U(t)|n\rangle=e^{-it(n+1/2)}|n\rangle$. Its classical endpoint is the identity at $t=2\pi$, because its Hamilton equations are $\dot Q=P$, $\dot P=-Q$ and make one full rotation, while by [F6] $$U(2\pi)|n\rangle=e^{-2\pi i(n+1/2)}|n\rangle=-|n\rangle$$ for every $n$. Completeness of the Hermite basis gives $U(2\pi)=-I$. For any $S$, choose a normalized lift $\widetilde M_S$ supplied by step 2.1. Then $\widetilde M_S$ and $-\widetilde M_S$ are two distinct lifts; step 2.3 proves there are no others. The kernel is exactly $\{I,-I\}$. [F4, F6, step 2.1, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 Fix $S_0$ and a normalized lift $M_0$. On a matrix neighborhood $\mathcal B$ of $S_0$ small enough that $SS_0^{-1}$ lies in the local neighborhood of [F4], put $\sigma(S)=L(SS_0^{-1})M_0$. The parameter path $(Y,A,X)\mapsto(\tau Y,I+\tau(A-I),\tau X)$ in [F4] joins each local factor lift to $I$ smoothly, with homogeneous quadratic logarithmic generator. Thus the local factors are endpoints of the piecewise-smooth subclass of the integrable class defining this group, so $\sigma(S)$ belongs to $\operatorname{Mp}$ and has endpoint $S$. Conversely the construction of [F4] writes any integrable-coefficient propagator endpoint as a finite product of these same local lifts. Hence allowing the broader integrable temporal class in the parity lemma introduces no additional endpoint operators or phases. It depends continuously on $S$, as does its inverse, pointwise in the Schwartz topology: the explicit chirp and linear-coordinate factors have uniformly bounded seminorm estimates on compact parameter neighborhoods, and the Fourier factors are fixed continuous maps. These estimates also justify continuity when composing such a varying local factor with a varying Schwartz vector. Step 3.1 shows every lift over $S$ is exactly $\sigma(S)$ or $-\sigma(S)$. [F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 The endpoint map is continuous for the specified operator topology, without assuming joint continuity of arbitrary Schwartz-operator composition. For each row $j$ and mode $k$, covariance and [F6] give $\langle R_jMg_0,Mg_{e_k}\rangle=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(S_{j,Q_k}+iS_{j,P_k})$, where the pairing is linear in its first argument. On the left $R_j$ is continuous on Schwartz space, its inclusion into $L^2$ is continuous, and only the two fixed input vectors $g_0,g_{e_k}$ are used. Thus every real matrix entry of $\pi(M)$ is continuous. Over $\mathcal B$, the scalar $\varepsilon(M):=\langle Mg_0,\sigma(\pi(M))g_0\rangle$ is continuous, takes exactly the values $+1,-1$, and distinguishes the two lifts since $\|g_0\|=1$. Therefore the two inverse images $\varepsilon^{-1}(1)$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}(-1)$ in $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal B)$ are disjoint open sheets; on each, $\pi$ and $\pm\sigma$ are continuous inverse maps onto $\mathcal B$. This proves the two-fold covering in the given topology. [F4, F6, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The same charts make the set a topological group. Locally its elements are $\varepsilon\sigma(S)$. Products and inverses of their explicit finite-parameter factors depend continuously on the matrix parameters and on each Schwartz vector, by the uniform seminorm bounds in step 4.1; their endpoint matrices multiply and invert continuously. The sign relative to a local section at the resulting endpoint is recovered by the continuous vacuum pairing in step 5.1. Hence multiplication and inversion are continuous in these charts, which have precisely the operator topology by step 5.1. Finally every defining normalized path is continuous in that topology by [F4], including its inverse path, so it joins its endpoint to $I$. Consequently the group is path connected. Together with step 3.1 this proves the connected double cover with kernel $\{I,-I\}$ and its defining unitary action, retaining the unrestricted phase ambiguity only for arbitrary individual Weyl implementers. [F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $r\geq1$,
$\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, $\beta>0$ in inverse joules, $c\in\mathbb R$ in
joules, and let $G=G^T$ be a strictly positive real $2r\times2r$ matrix
whose entries have units of inverse seconds. Assume $(U,V,\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r)$
is a finite diagonalization certificate for $G$ as defined earlier, with
each $\omega_j>0$ in inverse seconds. Let $H_{G,c}^{(0)}$ be the symmetric
quadratic operator on the stated Schwartz domain. Then its graph closure
$H:=\overline{H_{G,c}^{(0)}}$ exists and is self-adjoint, and its finite-mode
Gibbs partition sum is
$$Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})=e^{-\beta c}\prod_{j=1}^{r}\left[2\sinh\!\left(\frac{\beta\hbar\omega_j}{2}\right)\right]^{-1}\in(0,\infty),\qquad \sinh x:=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}{2}.$$
The matrix $G$ acts on the finite grouped quadratures; the bosonic Fock
space remains infinite-dimensional at each $r\geq1$. This conditional
finite-mode conclusion neither proves that every positive $G$ has a
diagonalization certificate nor asserts infinite-mode implementability,
interacting depletion bounds, or superfluidity.
items.proof:
1.1 By [F2], the certificate's matrices give a unitary $M$ satisfying $M^*R_gM=S_gR_g$ on the common transported Schwartz core. By [F3], we may take this implementer to preserve Schwartz space: its normalized metaplectic implementer has that property, and multiplying by a scalar phase leaves $M^*R_gM$ unchanged. [A1, A2, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Conjugating each symmetrically ordered term of $H_{G,c}^{(0)}$ by $M$ replaces $R_g$ by $S_gR_g$ . Collecting the finite sums gives $$M^*H_{G,c}^{(0)}M=\frac14\sum_{a,b}(S_g^TGS_g)_{ab}(R_{g,a}R_{g,b}+R_{g,b}R_{g,a})+cI.$$ By [A2] this is the diagonal quadratic with coefficient $D_\omega$ on the same core. [A2, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 On the finite Hermite core put $a_j=(Q_j+iP_j)/\sqrt{2\hbar}$ and $a_j^*=(Q_j-iP_j)/\sqrt{2\hbar}$ . The relation $[Q_j,P_j]=i\hbar I$ gives $Q_j^2+P_j^2=2\hbar(a_j^*a_j+\tfrac12 I)$ by direct multiplication. Consequently the diagonal quadratic is $\sum_j\hbar\omega_j(a_j^*a_j+\tfrac12 I)+cI$ . Write $g_{\mathbf n}\in L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ for the product Hermite basis and set $\phi_{\mathbf n}:=\mathcal U^{-1}g_{\mathbf n}\in\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)$ . Then $\mathcal U\phi_{\mathbf n}=g_{\mathbf n}$ , and the diagonal quadratic has eigenvalue $E_{\mathbf n}=c+\sum_j\hbar\omega_j(n_j+\tfrac12)$ . Denote this diagonal differential expression on $\mathcal S$ by $\widetilde T_\omega^{(0)}$ , and its Fock-space transport on $\mathcal D$ by $T_\omega^{(0)}:=\mathcal U^{-1}\widetilde T_\omega^{(0)}\mathcal U$ . [F1, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Put $\epsilon_j=\hbar\omega_j$ and let $A$ be the maximal diagonal multiplier in the basis $(\phi_{\mathbf n})$ with eigenvalues $\sum_j\epsilon_jn_j$ . By [F5], $A$ is self-adjoint on the domain where $\sum_{\mathbf n}|\sum_j\epsilon_jn_j|^2|f_{\mathbf n}|^2<\infty$ . The diagonal operator with eigenvalues $E_{\mathbf n}$ is $A+c_0I$ , where $c_0=c+\tfrac12\sum_j\epsilon_j$ . Its domain is the same: for real $x,c_0$ , $|x+c_0|^2\leq2|x|^2+2|c_0|^2$ and $|x|^2\leq2|x+c_0|^2+2|c_0|^2$ , and each coefficient sequence $(f_{\mathbf n})$ is in $\ell^2$ . For $g\in D((A+c_0I)^*)$ , [F7] says that boundedness of $f\mapsto\langle(A+c_0I)f,g\rangle$ and boundedness of $f\mapsto c_0\langle f,g\rangle$ imply boundedness of $f\mapsto\langle Af,g\rangle$ . Thus $g\in D(A^*)=D(A)$ and $(A+c_0I)^*g=Ag+c_0g$ . Conversely, every $g\in D(A)$ satisfies this adjoint identity, so $T=A+c_0I$ is self-adjoint. Finite Hermite truncations converge in its graph norm, because the tail of $\sum_{\mathbf n}(1+|E_{\mathbf n}|^2)|f_{\mathbf n}|^2$ tends to zero. Thus finite Hermite sums are a core for $T$ in the graph norm of [F8]. [A1, F5, F7, F8, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For $\psi\in\mathcal D$ , put $f=\mathcal U\psi\in\mathcal S$ . The coordinate expression $\widetilde T_\omega^{(0)}$ sends $f$ to an $L^2$ function. Integration by parts against each Schwartz Hermite function gives $\langle T_\omega^{(0)}\psi,\phi_{\mathbf n}\rangle =E_{\mathbf n}\langle\psi,\phi_{\mathbf n}\rangle$ ; equivalently, this is the $L^2$ pairing of the differential expression on $f$ with $g_{\mathbf n}=\mathcal U\phi_{\mathbf n}$ . Boundary terms vanish because both functions are Schwartz. For every finite set $F$ of occupation indices, orthogonal projection therefore gives $\sum_{\mathbf n\in F}|E_{\mathbf n}\langle\psi,\phi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2 \leq\|T_\omega^{(0)}\psi\|^2$ . These coefficients are square-summable, and completeness of $(\phi_{\mathbf n})$ from [F4] identifies their vector with $T_\omega^{(0)}\psi$ . Hence $\mathcal D\subseteq D(T)$ and the diagonal expression is $T$ on $\mathcal D$ . The finite Hermite sums from step 4.1 lie in $\mathcal D$ because [F1] places each $g_{\mathbf n}$ in $\mathcal S$ , and are graph-norm dense in $D(T)$ ; so the graph closure of this restriction is $T$. [F1, F4, F8, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 By step 1.1, $M$ and $M^*$ preserve Schwartz space, and by step 2.1 $H_{G,c}^{(0)}=M T_\omega^{(0)}M^*$ there. Step 5.1 gives graph closure $T$ for the diagonal restriction. Conjugation by the unitary $M$ carries the graph and its closure in $\mathcal F_s\oplus\mathcal F_s$ to the graph and closure of $H_{G,c}^{(0)}$ , so $H=\overline{H_{G,c}^{(0)}}=MTM^*$ . This is self-adjoint because $T$ is self-adjoint and $M$ is unitary. [F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Set $q_j=e^{-\beta\epsilon_j}=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_j}$ . Since $\beta>0$ and every $\omega_j>0$ , $0<q_j<1$ ; the mode set is finite, so $q_*<1$ and $\sum_jq_j<\infty$ . Apply [F5] to the diagonal number-energy operator $A$ to get $\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta A})=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty$ . On the occupation basis, $T$ has eigenvalues $E_{\mathbf n}=c_0+\sum_j\epsilon_jn_j$ , so the spectral exponential has positive eigenvalues $e^{-\beta E_{\mathbf n}}=e^{-\beta c_0}\prod_jq_j^{n_j}$ by [F9]. Thus $e^{-\beta T}=e^{-\beta c_0}e^{-\beta A}$ on the occupation basis; [F10] and the trace-class conclusion for $e^{-\beta A}$ from [F5] show that $e^{-\beta T}$ is positive trace class. Its eigenvalue sum is $e^{-\beta c_0}\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty$ by [F5], so [F6] identifies that sum with its trace. By steps 6.1 and 5.1, the vectors $M\phi_{\mathbf n}$ form a complete orthonormal eigenbasis for $H$ with the same eigenvalues; equivalently $e^{-\beta H}=M e^{-\beta T}M^*$ . The unitary invariance in [F10] makes $e^{-\beta H}$ trace class with the same eigenvalue sum, and [F6] gives the same trace. Finally, $$e^{-\beta c_0}\prod_j(1-e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_j})^{-1}=e^{-\beta c}\prod_j\frac{e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_j/2}}{1-e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_j}}=e^{-\beta c}\prod_j\left[2\sinh\!\left(\frac{\beta\hbar\omega_j}{2}\right)\right]^{-1}.$$ Every factor is strictly positive and finite, proving $Z_\beta\in(0,\infty)$ . The only infinite-dimensional Hilbert space used here is the bosonic Fock space for the stated finite number $r$ of modes. [A1, F4, F5, F6, F9, F10, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎
items.remarks:
The proof uses the finite-mode quadrature conventions of
[[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]], the occupation and Hermite core
identification of [[lem-nrqmx-finite-mode-fock-schr-identification]], the
individual Bogoliubov implementer of [[thm-nrqmx-finite-mode-bogoliubov]],
and the Schwartz-preserving normalized implementer of
[[thm-nrqmx-finite-metaplectic-construction]] at the exact interfaces in
[F1]–[F4]. These are mathematical supplier uses; the theorem remains
conditional on its explicit diagonalization certificate and hypotheses.
Run-readiness records are separate operational evidence and are not
mathematical premises or independent proof approval.
